requirements: Reproduce the core contributions of 'Rethinking Latency Denial-of-Service: Attacking the LLM Serving Framework, Not the Model', including the demonstration that existing model-centric latency attacks are ineffective under continuous batching, the design and implementation of the Fill and Squeeze (F&S) attack, the black-box KV cache side-channel probing mechanism, and the empirical results showing TTFT/TPOT slowdowns with reduced attack cost.

sub_tasks.requirements: The LLM serving environment (vLLM v0.11.2, target models, hardware, and configuration) has been provisioned correctly to reproduce the paper's experiments.
Hardware provisioning matches the paper's server: an NVIDIA GPU node with L40S (48GB VRAM) devices, up to 8 GPUs available for scaling experiments.

Code has been implemented that detects and requires NVIDIA L40S (or equivalent 48GB) GPUs at runtime and fails fast (or logs a warning) when the reported VRAM per device is not ~48GB, matching the single-GPU experimental base.
Code has been implemented that supports launching experiments on 1, 2, 4, and 8 GPUs of the 8xL40S server to accommodate TP1/TP2/TP4/TP8 experiments referenced in Section 6.4.2.
The vLLM serving framework is installed and instantiated at version v0.11.2 with the paper's core configuration.
Code has been implemented that installs and verifies vLLM v0.11.2 (e.g., via `pip show vllm` or `vllm.__version__`) before starting the serving process, aborting if the version does not match.
The vLLM server is launched with `gpu_memory_utilization=0.90` so that ~90% of GPU VRAM is reserved for model weights and KV cache, matching Section 4 and Section 6.1.

The vLLM server is configured to use continuous batching with PagedAttention (default v1 scheduler) without disabling preemption, so that the serving-layer behaviors under study (FCFS admission, LIFO preemption, recomputation) are active.

Code has been implemented that configures the concurrent request limit (max_num_seqs / batch size) to 16 for the Section 4 continuous-batching study while allowing higher concurrency for main experiments.

Code has been implemented that launches vLLM with configurable `tensor_parallel_size` in {1, 2, 4, 8} via CLI flags so the same server-launch script supports both single-GPU main experiments and multi-GPU scalability experiments.

The serving stack exposes per-request timing (TTFT, per-token ITL, TPOT) and scheduler event traces (preemption count, running/waiting queue sizes, KV cache usage) via vLLM logging or Prometheus metrics for downstream measurement.
The three target open-source models are acquired and served with matching identifiers and generation configurations.
Code has been implemented that downloads and loads Qwen3-8B (HuggingFace `Qwen/Qwen3-8B`) into vLLM with its standard chat template.
Code has been implemented that downloads and loads Gemma3-12B-it (HuggingFace `google/gemma-3-12b-it`) into vLLM with its standard chat template.
Code has been implemented that downloads and loads DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (HuggingFace `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B`) into vLLM with its standard chat template.

Code has been implemented that supports a reasoning-mode configuration for Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (enabling chain-of-thought / thinking traces) as required by the Section 6.4.3 experiments.

The default sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens) used at serving time are set consistently across models per Appendix A to permit fair latency comparison; max output length is configured to allow long generations that reach the ~5000-8000 output-token range observed in Fig. 3c.
A client-side harness for issuing multi-tenant concurrent requests to the vLLM server has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that talks to vLLM via its OpenAI-compatible HTTP API (`/v1/chat/completions` with streaming) to obtain per-token timestamps needed for computing TTFT, ITL, and TPOT.
Code has been implemented that spawns multiple concurrent client identities (distinct API keys or user IDs) to emulate co-located malicious and benign tenants, matching the threat model in Section 3.
Reproducibility scaffolding (dependency pinning, seeding, and launch scripts) has been provided so that experiments can be re-executed.
Code has been implemented that pins the Python, CUDA, PyTorch, and vLLM versions (e.g., a `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`) consistent with vLLM v0.11.2's supported stack.

Launch scripts (shell or Python) exist that start the vLLM server with the exact flags for each model/TP configuration used in Sections 4, 6.2-6.4, so a single command reproduces each experimental serving setup.
Code has been implemented that sets random seeds for the client-side workload generator and probing model so runs are reproducible, while leaving server-side vLLM scheduling stochasticity intact.
Datasets (Alpaca, ShareGPT, BurstGPT) and traffic generators (Poisson arrivals, real-world traces, benign vs. malicious mixing) have been prepared to drive attack experiments.
Benign-user prompt datasets (Alpaca and ShareGPT) have been acquired and preprocessed for use as normal traffic.

Code has been implemented to download/load the Stanford Alpaca instruction-following dataset (tatsu-lab/stanford_alpaca or equivalent) and expose prompts as an iterable prompt pool for the benign-user request generator.
Code has been implemented to load the ShareGPT (Vicuna) conversation dataset and extract user turns as prompts for long-context benign traffic in the ablation study.

Prompt preprocessing (tokenization with the target model's tokenizer, filtering by minimum/maximum length, and shuffling with a fixed seed) has been implemented so that Alpaca and ShareGPT yield reproducible prompt streams with distinct short-context vs. long-context profiles as described in Section 6.3.2.
The real-world BurstGPT trace has been acquired and processed into Low/Medium/High traffic-intensity windows for Section 6.4.1.
Code has been implemented to download and parse the BurstGPT dataset (10.31M real conversation traces) into per-hour request arrival counts.
Code has been implemented to segment BurstGPT traffic into the three representative windows used in Figure 11: Low intensity at 01:00, Medium intensity at 20:00, and High intensity at 16:00.
The extracted BurstGPT intensity levels reproduce the paper's reported conversation rates within a small tolerance: Low approx 13.7 conv/h, Medium approx 47.9 conv/h, and High approx 115.1 conv/h.
A configurable traffic generator that emits benign and malicious requests to the vLLM endpoint has been implemented.
Code has been implemented to generate benign request arrivals following a Poisson process with a configurable request rate, matching the workload model in Section 6.1.

Code has been implemented to mix benign and malicious requests according to a configurable malicious-user rate parameter (supporting at least the values 25%, 50%, 75%, and 90% used in Section 6.3.1) while keeping the total request rate constant.

Code has been implemented to replay BurstGPT-derived hourly arrival patterns as benign traffic, so that Low/Medium/High traces from Section 6.4.1 can be injected while attack traffic runs concurrently at a fixed malicious ratio (50%).

The traffic generator dispatches requests concurrently over the vLLM HTTP/OpenAI-compatible API with multiple client identities so that per-user latency (TTFT, TPOT, ITL) can be measured independently for benign and malicious cohorts.
The traffic generator accepts a random seed and produces deterministic, reproducible arrival timings and prompt selections given identical configuration inputs.

Code has been implemented to configure and run the three workload scenarios used in the paper (Poisson-Alpaca main workload, ShareGPT ablation workload, and BurstGPT real-world workload) through a single unified experiment driver, so downstream attack/evaluation modules can select workloads by configuration.
The baseline latency attacks (Engorgio, LoopLLM, ExtendAttack, and plain-text prompts) used for comparison have been re-implemented and produce prompts consistent with the paper.
Engorgio white-box optimization attack has been re-implemented following the paper's description of EOS-suppression + adversarial objective on a surrogate model with prompt transfer to the target.
Code has been implemented that provides an Engorgio prompt generator module exposing an interface to produce a batch of adversarial prompts targeting a specified surrogate causal LM.

Code has been implemented that composes the Engorgio optimization loss as a weighted sum of an EOS-suppression term (minimizing P(EOS) at each step), an adversarial randomness term L_adv, and an auxiliary F_aux term as described in Section 2.3.
Code has been implemented that performs gradient-based token-level optimization over the input prompt for Engorgio and returns the finalized adversarial prompt after convergence or budget exhaustion.
When run against the target models in Table 1, the Engorgio baseline produces mean output token length consistent with Fig. 3c (approximately 2836 tokens on average).
LoopLLM white-box repetitive-generation attack has been re-implemented consistent with the referenced paper and reproduces its reported prompt behavior in this setup.
Code has been implemented for a LoopLLM prompt generator that optimizes prompts to trap the target model in repetitive-generation loops that postpone EOS.

Code has been implemented that iteratively refines LoopLLM prompts using gradient-based token substitution on a surrogate model and supports transfer to target models such as Qwen3-8B and Gemma3-12B-it.
LoopLLM baseline achieves an average output length on Qwen3-8B consistent with Fig. 3c (approximately 7469 tokens).
ExtendAttack black-box prompt-engineering attack has been re-implemented to induce recursive/verbose generation without requiring model gradients.
Code has been implemented that provides an ExtendAttack prompt generator producing prompts that leverage instruction-following to force recursive explanations or exhaustive enumerations.
Code has been implemented that supports ExtendAttack being used both standalone (as a baseline) and as a pluggable payload inside the F&S tiered-prompt arsenal.
ExtendAttack baseline produces average output length on Qwen3-8B consistent with Fig. 3c (approximately 5937 tokens).
The plain-text prompt attack baseline (natural, non-adversarial instructions designed to induce long generations) has been re-implemented as described in Section 4.1 and 5.2.1.

Code has been implemented that assembles a plain-text prompt collection of natural-language instructions (e.g., 'write a story where every sentence must be followed by a 50-word analysis of its own grammar') targeting logically expensive generation paths.
Plain-text prompts are structured as parameterized templates T(s) with variable seeds s (topics, numbers) so many concrete prompts can be sampled from a single template as described in Section 5.2.1.
Plain-text prompts on Qwen3-8B produce mean input length of approximately 46 tokens (Fig. 3b) and mean output length of approximately 4693 tokens (Fig. 3c).

A unified baseline attack driver has been implemented that dispatches any of the four baseline attacks (Engorgio, LoopLLM, ExtendAttack, plain-text) against a running vLLM endpoint using a common interface.
Code has been implemented exposing a common `AttackMethod` interface with a method that returns the next adversarial prompt string, implemented by each of the four baselines.

Code has been implemented that dispatches baseline attack prompts using a fixed-interval injection policy (as specified in Section 6.1) so all baselines are compared under the scheduler-oblivious regime.
Code has been implemented that logs per-attack per-request metadata (prompt tokens, output tokens, wall-clock latencies) for downstream cost and effectiveness analysis.
The pre-computed adversarial prompt corpora for the optimization-based baselines are produced once and cached for reuse in all downstream experiments to ensure reproducibility.
Code has been implemented that serializes generated Engorgio and LoopLLM prompts (with their input/output token statistics) to disk for reuse across attack runs.
Code has been implemented that loads cached baseline prompt corpora and samples from them uniformly at random during each attack slot.
Baseline input-length statistics match the paper's Fig. 3b measurements.

Mean input token length across the produced Engorgio, LoopLLM, ExtendAttack, and plain-text prompt corpora matches the values reported in Fig. 3b within a reasonable tolerance (Engorgio ~5181, LoopLLM ~399, ExtendAttack ~172, plain-text ~46, in tokens).
The cost formalization for white-box, black-box, and plain-text attacks and empirical cost/token-length comparisons from Fig. 3 have been reproduced.
The three attack cost paradigms (white-box, black-box, plain-text) have been formalized as computable cost functions.
Code has been implemented to compute the white-box attack cost as Cost_wb = T_opt * P_avg * p_e, taking optimization time, average GPU power, and unit electricity price as inputs.

Code has been implemented to compute the black-box attack cost as Cost_bb = sum over N_query iterations of (H_{i,j} * p_i + H_{o,j} * p_o), summing per-iteration input and output token counts multiplied by the input and output token unit prices.
Code has been implemented to compute the plain-text single-shot cost as Cost_pt = H_i * p_i + H_o * p_o, corresponding to a one-time query and response.
Cost calibration inputs (GPT-4o mini token pricing and industrial electricity benchmarks) have been sourced and applied.
Code has been implemented to load GPT-4o mini per-token input/output prices (p_i, p_o) from a configuration source and use them in all black-box and plain-text cost computations.

Code has been implemented to load an industrial electricity price (p_e, USD/kWh, e.g., from EIA Virginia industrial sector benchmark) and combine it with GPU average power to compute white-box compute cost.
Per-attack cost and time measurements for Engorgio, LoopLLM, AutoDoS, ExtendAttack, and plain-text prompts have been collected.

Code has been implemented to run each of the five baseline attack methods (Engorgio, LoopLLM, AutoDoS, ExtendAttack, plain-text prompts) end-to-end and record wall-clock time cost (seconds) and cumulative token counts per generated prompt.

Code has been implemented to convert per-attack raw measurements into economic cost in USD by applying the corresponding cost formula (white-box for Engorgio/LoopLLM, black-box for AutoDoS, plain-text for ExtendAttack and plain-text prompts).
Code has been implemented to log per-attack input token length distributions (mean and standard deviation) across generated prompts for downstream comparison with Fig. 3b.
Code has been implemented to log per-attack output token length distributions (mean and standard deviation) produced by the target LLM for each attack method for comparison with Fig. 3c.
Fig. 3 subplots (cost-vs-time scatter, input token length distribution, output token length distribution) have been reproduced.

Code has been implemented to plot Fig. 3a as a scatter of Economic Cost (USD, log scale) vs. Time Cost (s, log scale) with distinct markers for Engorgio, LoopLLM, AutoDoS, ExtendAttack, and plain-text prompts.
Code has been implemented to plot Fig. 3b and Fig. 3c as bar/box charts of mean input and mean output token length per attack method with standard deviation error indicators.
Quantitative claims from Section 4.1 and Fig. 3 have been numerically verified.
The measured economic and time cost of plain-text prompts is 100x-500x lower than optimization-based attacks (Engorgio, LoopLLM, AutoDoS) as reported in Section 4.1.
The measured mean input token length for AutoDoS matches the reported ~5181 tokens (with standard deviation ~414) shown in Fig. 3b within tolerance.
The measured mean input token length for plain-text prompts is on the order of ~46 tokens (Fig. 3b) and is substantially shorter than AutoDoS while producing comparable output lengths.

The measured mean output token lengths for Engorgio, LoopLLM, AutoDoS, ExtendAttack, and plain-text prompts fall in the ranges reported in Fig. 3c (e.g., AutoDoS ~7469, plain-text ~4693) within tolerance.

The empirical analysis showing that model-centric latency attacks yield marginal TTFT impact and only slight TPOT degradation under continuous batching (Fig. 4) plus the CUDA kernel profiling (Fig. 5) have been reproduced.
The multi-tenant experiment measuring the impact of a scheduler-oblivious latency attack (LoopLLM) on normal user metrics across varying malicious ratios (Fig. 4) has been implemented and executed.

The experiment harness composition (Qwen3-8B on a single L40S with gpu_memory_utilization=0.9, batch size 16, LoopLLM as the injected malicious workload, benign requests) has been implemented as described in Section 4.2.
Code has been implemented to launch a vLLM server hosting Qwen3-8B on a single NVIDIA L40S (48GB) GPU with gpu_memory_utilization=0.9 for this Section 4.2 experiment.

Code has been implemented to drive a concurrency of 16 request threads (total in-flight requests) against the vLLM endpoint, mixing benign Alpaca-style requests with malicious LoopLLM prompts at configurable malicious-request ratios (e.g., 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%).
Code has been implemented to collect per-request TTFT and TPOT for benign requests only (filtering out malicious attacker requests) so that co-located user impact is measured cleanly.
Measured co-located-user latency observations from Section 4.2 / Fig. 4 have been reproduced.

Under the LoopLLM attack on Qwen3-8B with 50%-75% malicious requests, the increase in total end-to-end latency for benign requests relative to the no-attack baseline is bounded to the paper's reported 3-5.7% range (i.e., total latency moves from ~7s to ~8s, not orders of magnitude).
The benign-user TTFT under LoopLLM at 50-75% malicious ratio on Qwen3-8B remains largely unchanged relative to the no-attack baseline (matching the paper's claim that TTFT is nearly unaffected).

The benign-user TPOT under LoopLLM shows a consistent (but modest) degradation as the malicious ratio increases, matching the qualitative trend from Fig. 4 (TPOT grows with malicious ratio while TTFT does not).
Code has been implemented to produce the Fig. 4-style visualization plotting benign-user TTFT and TPOT (with distributions/error bars) as a function of malicious-request ratio.
The micro-architectural CUDA kernel profiling under latency attack that produces Fig. 5 has been reproduced, isolating the memory-bound attention kernel as the source of contagious TPOT degradation.
Code has been implemented to invoke a CUDA kernel profiler (e.g., Nsight Systems, nvprof, or torch.profiler with CUDA activities) while running vLLM under the attack workload from Section 4.2.

Code has been implemented to parse profiler output and aggregate per-kernel execution durations across the tracked kernels including the FlashAttention decode kernel (flash_fwd_splitkv_kernel), rms_norm, and elementwise kernels.

Code has been implemented to sweep system load (e.g., varying number of concurrent attack requests or KV-cache occupancy levels) and record kernel durations at each load level so that trends can be plotted.
Code has been implemented to generate a stacked/lined plot (Fig. 5 style) of kernel execution durations vs. load, breaking down attention vs. rms_norm vs. elementwise contributions.
The measured execution duration of compute-bound kernels (rms_norm, elementwise) stays approximately constant across load levels (matching the flat trend in Fig. 5).

The measured execution duration of the FlashAttention decode kernel (flash_fwd_splitkv_kernel) exhibits heavy-tailed growth as attack-induced KV cache pressure rises, dominating total kernel time at high load (matching the surge in Fig. 5).

Ancillary baseline attacks (Engorgio, ExtendAttack, plain-text) have been verified to produce similarly marginal collateral impact under continuous batching (per the paper's statement that 'other attacks have similar effects').
Code has been implemented to rerun the Section 4.2 co-located-user experiment on Qwen3-8B with at least one additional baseline attack (Engorgio, ExtendAttack, or plain-text) in place of LoopLLM.

For the additional baseline attack(s), the observed benign-user TTFT remains close to the no-attack baseline (order-of-magnitude smaller than the F&S-induced TTFT surges reported later), confirming the paper's claim of general ineffectiveness of model-centric attacks under CB.
The paper's characterization of vLLM's BlockSpaceManager, FCFS admission, KV saturation, LIFO preemption, and swap/recomputation recovery penalties has been validated on the target vLLM version.
Instrumentation of the vLLM scheduler internals (WAITING/RUNNING queues, BlockSpaceManager, free_block_queue, preemption hooks) required for reverse-engineering has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that patches or instruments vLLM v0.11.2's Scheduler class to log per-iteration WAITING queue length, RUNNING queue length, and the free_block_queue size / number of free KV blocks.

Code has been implemented that intercepts BlockSpaceManager.can_allocate() (or equivalent v1 API) calls to record per-iteration admission decisions (success/failure) for the head-of-line request in the WAITING queue.

Code has been implemented that hooks Scheduler._preempt() (or the v1 equivalent) to log each preemption event with a timestamp, victim request id, iteration index, and recovery mode (swap vs recomputation).

Code has been implemented that exports per-iteration global KV-cache occupancy (used_blocks / total_blocks) as a time series aligned with request-level events, forming the ground-truth trace used throughout the reverse-engineering study.
FCFS admission behavior and memory-based Head-of-Line blocking (Section 5.1.1) have been reproduced and verified on the target vLLM deployment.

A driver script has been implemented that submits an ordered mixture of large (memory-heavy) requests followed by many small requests to the vLLM server so that the head-of-line request in the WAITING queue cannot be allocated while smaller pending requests could fit in the remaining num_batched_tokens budget.

The scheduler admission-loop code path has been verified to terminate scheduling for the current iteration as soon as can_allocate() fails for the head-of-line WAITING request, i.e., strict FCFS ordering is preserved and later smaller requests are not admitted out of order.

Code has been implemented that, under the HOL-blocking scenario, records the queueing wait time of each subsequent small request from submission until it is finally admitted to the RUNNING queue and demonstrates non-trivial stall while the free_block_queue is depleted.

Under the HOL-blocking experiment, the measured stalled TTFT of benign short requests while the free_block_queue is exhausted matches the paper's description of memory-based HOL blocking on the order of seconds to tens of seconds (consistent with the F&S TTFT inflation reported in Table 1).
KV-cache saturation dynamics (monotonic growth of RUNNING requests' KV footprint and depletion of free_block_queue) have been characterized on the target deployment.

Code has been implemented that generates a controlled long-output workload and records, per iteration, the number of physical KV blocks allocated to each RUNNING request, confirming monotonic growth during the decoding phase.

Code has been implemented that identifies the empirical saturation threshold C_sat (fraction of total KV blocks at which admission via can_allocate() first begins to fail) on the configured gpu_memory_utilization=0.90 setup, and stores it as a reproducible constant used by later attack code.
LIFO preemption policy and reinsertion at the front of the WAITING queue (Section 5.1.2) have been validated on the target vLLM version.

A test harness has been implemented that submits a sequence of long-running requests in a known temporal order, drives the system into a preemption event, and records which request id is selected as the victim by _preempt().
The recorded preemption victims match a Last-In-First-Out policy: the most recently scheduled (latest-admitted) RUNNING request is selected as the victim in the observed preemption events.

The instrumentation confirms that a preempted victim is prepended to the front of the WAITING queue (rather than discarded or appended), so that on the next admission cycle it is the first candidate re-admitted.
Recovery penalties for swap and recomputation modes (Section 5.1.2 bullets, Figure 6) have been characterized on the target vLLM version.

Code has been implemented to configure and run vLLM in the recomputation preemption mode (as used by the unified v1 scheduler / v0.11.2 default) and to record, per preempted request, the additional prefill cost incurred upon recovery.

Code has been implemented that, for the swapping-based recovery path (legacy vLLM behavior), measures the wall-clock cost of migrating KV blocks between GPU VRAM and CPU host memory over PCIe for a preempted request.

The measured recovery cost per preemption event is quantitatively larger than the incremental memory-pressure cost required to trigger the preemption, confirming the asymmetric attacker/defender cost described in Section 5.1.2.

Code has been implemented that, when a request is preempted under recomputation mode, verifies that its KV-cache blocks are freed and that upon re-admission the engine reprocesses the full prompt plus previously generated tokens (i.e., decoding is restarted from prefill).

The end-to-end scheduler state-transition model of Figure 6 (WAITING <-> RUNNING transitions gated by can_allocate() and _preempt()) has been reproduced as an executable trace on the target deployment.

Code has been implemented that produces a time-aligned event log (admission successes, admission failures due to memory, preemption events, re-admissions of preempted victims) matching the state-machine depicted in Figure 6.

Code has been implemented that generates a summary figure/table (per the visualization used in Figure 9 top rows: KV usage, scheduler events, running/waiting queue sizes) from the recorded scheduler traces to enable direct visual comparison with the paper's Figure 6/9 characterization.
The tiered prompt arsenal (P_High, P_Mid, P_Low) with pluggable payloads (plain-text and ExtendAttack) achieving the required expansion ratios has been implemented.
Pluggable payload abstraction supporting plain-text and ExtendAttack payloads has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines parameterized prompt templates T(s) accepting a variable seed (e.g., a random topic or number) so that different concrete prompt instances can be generated from a shared template.

Code has been implemented that exposes a payload-selection interface so the attack orchestrator can plug in either plain-text prompts or ExtendAttack prompts as the underlying payload for the same tiered structure.

Code has been implemented that constructs plain-text prompts using expansion-logic instructions (e.g., 'Write a story where every sentence must be followed by a 50-word analysis of its own grammar') that induce long, coherent, non-adversarial generations.
Code has been implemented that constructs ExtendAttack-style payloads (per the ExtendAttack baseline) and wraps them in the same tiered-prompt interface used by plain-text payloads.
Tiered prompt categorization (P_High, P_Mid, P_Low) based on KV-cache/output-length consumption has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that exposes three distinct prompt tiers (P_High, P_Mid, P_Low), each retrievable as a separate pool that the Fill/Squeeze orchestrator can sample from.

Code has been implemented that assigns each prompt to a tier based on its expected output-length band: P_High targets near-Lmax generations, P_Mid targets moderate ~1k-2k token generations, and P_Low targets short but non-trivial ~500 token generations.
Code has been implemented that routes P_High prompts to the Fill phase for rapid VRAM occupation and routes P_Low prompts to the Squeeze phase to tip a near-saturated system over the boundary.
Code has been implemented that uses P_Mid prompts as a buffer during transitional states to maintain memory pressure between Fill and Squeeze cycles so the system does not recover excess capacity.
Empirical validation that constructed prompts achieve the tier-specific output length / expansion behavior claimed by the paper.

Code has been implemented to measure and log the input token length and output token length for each generated prompt/response pair so that expansion ratio R = L_out / L_in can be computed per prompt.

Plain-text prompts produce output token lengths in the same order-of-magnitude range as optimization-based baselines while using significantly shorter inputs, matching the distribution shown in Figure 3b-3c (mean input ~46 tokens, mean output ~4693 tokens for plain-text).
P_High prompts empirically drive generation to near the model's maximum output limit (L_out approaching L_max) on the target models.
P_Mid prompts empirically produce output sequences in the moderate ~1k-2k token range as specified in Section 5.2.1.
P_Low prompts empirically produce short but non-trivial output sequences of approximately 500 tokens as specified in Section 5.2.1.
The tiered prompt arsenal exposes an API usable by later Fill/Squeeze phases and probing.

Code has been implemented that provides a sampling function returning a fresh prompt of a requested tier (High/Mid/Low) and payload type (plain-text/ExtendAttack) so upstream orchestration and side-channel probing can request prompts by (tier, payload).
Code has been implemented so that repeated sampling from a tier yields diverse prompt instances (e.g., via varying seeds s in T(s)) to avoid trivial duplication across concurrent injection threads.
The black-box KV-cache side-channel probe using ITL sequences and a LightGBM regressor/classifier has been implemented and validated against ground-truth KV usage as in Fig. 8.
The ITL probing data collection infrastructure that periodically dispatches low-intensity probe requests and records inter-token latency sequences has been implemented.

Code has been implemented to send periodic probe requests drawn from the low-intensity prompt pool (P_Low, ~500-token outputs) at a configurable interval to the target vLLM server via its OpenAI-compatible streaming API.

Code has been implemented to parse the streaming response of a probe request and record per-token timestamps to produce a per-request ITL vector (time differences between consecutive generated tokens).
Code has been implemented to aggregate ITL vectors from probe requests into fixed-length feature windows t suitable for input to the LightGBM model, with configurable window size and stride.
Ground-truth KV-cache occupancy collection from vLLM has been implemented so that ITL observations can be paired with the true system state U_sys for training and validation.

Code has been implemented to read the global KV-cache usage from vLLM (e.g., via the /metrics Prometheus endpoint field vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc, or by instrumenting BlockSpaceManager to expose free_block_queue occupancy) at high frequency during probing.

Code has been implemented to time-align ITL vectors from probe requests with the corresponding ground-truth KV-cache utilization sampled during the probe's decoding window and to persist (t, U_sys) pairs to a training dataset file.

Code has been implemented to discretize KV usage into the ten bins used in Figure 8b ([1,5), [5,9), [9,14), [14,18), [18,23), [23,27), [27,31), [31,36), [36,40), [40,45)) for classification-based training/evaluation.
A LightGBM-based estimator M_theta that maps ITL vectors t to an estimate of global KV-cache usage U_sys has been implemented and trained.
Code has been implemented that instantiates a LightGBM model (LGBMRegressor and/or LGBMClassifier following Ke et al. 2017) and fits it on the collected (ITL-vector, KV-usage) training set.
Code has been implemented to serialize the trained LightGBM model to disk and reload it for online inference during attack orchestration.

The trained M_theta produces per-inference predictions in sub-millisecond time (excluding probe collection), enabling near-real-time synchronization with the Fill/Squeeze attack loop as stated in Section 5.2.2.
The online probing interface used by the attacker's control loop has been implemented so that Phases III/IV can query estimated KV usage U_hat_sys = M_theta(t).
Code has been implemented that exposes a function/API returning the current estimated KV usage and the memory gap Delta_mem = C_sat - M_theta(t) for use by the Fill/Squeeze decision logic.
Code has been implemented to continuously refresh the ITL window t as new probe tokens arrive and to update U_hat_sys asynchronously without blocking the attack dispatcher.
Validation experiments and figures reproducing Figure 8 (per-user ITL trends, ITL-vs-KV heatmap, and prediction trace) on Qwen3-8B have been implemented.
Code has been implemented to generate the per-user ITL trend plot (Fig. 8a) showing synchronized ITL increases across ~20 co-located tenants as global KV-cache usage rises.
Code has been implemented to produce the ITL-vs-KV-usage heatmap (Fig. 8b) binning KV usage into the ten ranges from [1,5) through [40,45) and reporting mean ITL per bin.
Code has been implemented to plot the time-series trace of predicted vs. ground-truth KV-cache usage (Fig. 8c) over an attack episode on Qwen3-8B.
The measured ITL-vs-KV-usage relation on Qwen3-8B shows a strong positive linear correlation (monotonically increasing mean ITL across the ten KV-usage bins), consistent with Figure 8b.

The trained LightGBM probe's predicted KV-usage trace tracks the ground-truth KV-usage trace on Qwen3-8B closely across both gradual accumulation and abrupt release events, as visualized in Figure 8c.

Code has been implemented to compute and report a quantitative fidelity metric (classification accuracy over the ten KV-usage bins and/or MAE/R^2 of the regressor) for the probe on the held-out Qwen3-8B validation trace.
Robustness and calibration behavior of the probing mechanism have been validated as claimed in Section 5.2.2.

Code has been implemented to measure the variance of predicted KV usage under stochastic scheduling noise (e.g., varying benign background traffic) and confirm minimal variance as reported in Fig. 8b/c.

Code has been implemented to calibrate the saturation constant C_sat (fraction of KV cache at which admission control triggers HOL blocking) for the target deployment, exposing it to downstream Fill/Squeeze phases.
The constrained-optimization formulation, closed-loop Fill/Squeeze control policy, and adaptive back-off have been implemented and integrated with prompt tiers and probing.
Phase III cost-optimal attack formulation as a constrained optimization problem over a time horizon T has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that models each attack action p_t as a composition of input length L_in and expected output length L_out with unit prices alpha and beta, and computes the per-action monetary cost accordingly.
Code has been implemented that defines the time-averaged cost objective (1/T) * sum_t cost(p_t) minimized over the action sequence.

Code has been implemented that enforces the saturation constraint M_theta(t_t) + E(p_t) >= C_sat - delta at each step, where E(p_t) is the expected KV memory expansion of prompt p_t and delta is a small saturation margin.

Code has been implemented that estimates E(p_t) (expected memory expansion) for each tiered prompt in {P_High, P_Mid, P_Low}, so the optimizer can select the cheapest prompt meeting the saturation constraint.

The optimizer prefers low-intensity prompts (P_Low) over high-intensity prompts (P_High) whenever the saturation constraint can still be satisfied, so the time-averaged cost is strictly less than a policy that always issues P_High.
The formulation exposes C_sat (KV saturation threshold) and delta (safety margin) as configurable parameters used by both the optimizer and the runtime controller.
Phase IV closed-loop feedback controller that integrates probing, Fill/Squeeze decisions, and adaptive back-off has been implemented.

Code has been implemented for a periodic probing loop that dispatches probe requests p_probe (sampled from P_Low), collects the returned ITL vector t, and feeds it into the pre-trained LightGBM model M_theta to obtain the KV-cache usage estimate.
Code has been implemented that computes the memory gap Delta_mem = C_sat - M_theta(t) on every control tick and exposes it to the injection policy.

Code has been implemented for the Fill decision branch: when Delta_mem is large (system idle), the controller dispatches high-intensity prompts from P_High to rapidly occupy the free_block_queue and induce HOL blocking.

Code has been implemented for the Squeeze decision branch: when Delta_mem approaches 0, the controller switches to low-intensity prompts from P_Low to tip the system over the saturation boundary and trigger preemption.
Code has been implemented that uses P_Mid as a buffer during transitional states to maintain memory pressure and prevent the system from recovering excess capacity between Fill and Squeeze cycles.

The controller decision policy is a pure function of the probed Delta_mem and configured thresholds so that identical probe traces produce identical Fill/Mid/Squeeze action sequences (deterministic given fixed random seeds).
Adaptive back-off logic that protects attack requests from being preempted has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that detects the over-saturation condition Delta_mem < 0 from the probe estimate and triggers a back-off state.

During back-off, the controller pauses new injections, waits for the system to recover a legitimate preempted request, and resumes injection immediately once probing indicates the victim has been re-admitted.
The back-off mechanism reduces the count of attacker-owned requests observed in vLLM's _preempt() victims relative to a no-back-off variant on the same trace.
End-to-end integration of Phases I-IV (tiered prompts, ITL probing, cost-optimal decision, adaptive back-off) into a runnable orchestrator has been implemented and validated.

The orchestrator loads the tiered prompt arsenal (P_High, P_Mid, P_Low) from Phase I and the trained LightGBM probe from Phase II via well-defined interfaces, without hard-coding them into the control loop.
The orchestrator supports pluggable underlying payloads (plain-text and ExtendAttack) selected via a configuration flag, matching the F&S+plain-text and F&S+ExtendAttack variants reported in Table 1.

The orchestrator exposes concurrency controls compatible with the paper's threat model (multiple attack identities under API quotas) and issues requests through the standard vLLM API without privileged access.

When run against the standard vLLM+Qwen3-8B setup with continuous batching, the orchestrator produces the temporal event pattern shown in Fig. 9: (1) a Fill ramp during which KV-cache usage rises to and pins at the High (97.5-100%) band, (2) a sustained Squeeze phase with a dense sequence of _preempt() events and sawtooth KV-cache traces, and (3) a growing Waiting queue while the Running queue stays saturated.

The average monetary cost per unit time of the integrated F&S orchestrator is lower than a fixed-interval baseline that always samples from P_High under matched injection duration, verifying the cost-optimal design.

On reasoning-configured DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, F&S+plain-text achieves TTFT of approximately 1.10 s, TPOT of approximately 67.47 ms, and cost of approximately $0.93 (Table 3).

Engorgio baseline under reasoning mode produces negligible latency impact (TTFT approximately 0.10 s on both Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) while incurring the highest attacker cost (approximately $1.23 and $1.13 respectively) among methods in Table 3.

depends_on: Main Attack Effectiveness Results (Table 1 and Fig. 9)

sub_tasks.requirements: The evaluation of perplexity filters, output-length caps, fairness/priority schedulers, and behavioral analysis against F&S has been reproduced.
Perplexity-based input filtering has been implemented and evaluated against F&S attack payloads.

Code has been implemented for a perplexity filter that computes prompt perplexity using a reference language model and rejects inputs above a configurable threshold trained on both perplexity and token length.

Code has been implemented that runs the perplexity filter over the F&S plain-text prompts, F&S+ExtendAttack prompts, and optimization-based baseline prompts (Engorgio/LoopLLM) and records the acceptance/rejection decision for each.

The perplexity filter blocks optimization-based adversarial prompts (Engorgio-style) at a substantially higher rate than F&S plain-text prompts, confirming that plain-text F&S prompts bypass perplexity-based filtering.
Output-length caps as a countermeasure have been implemented and evaluated against F&S.
Code has been implemented that enforces a configurable `max_tokens` output-length cap on each generation and re-runs the F&S attack under progressively tighter caps.

Code has been implemented to log TTFT, TPOT, and preemption counts under output-length caps and to compare them against uncapped baselines, quantifying the trade-off between attack mitigation and utility loss for long-context tasks.
Fairness-aware and priority-queue schedulers as countermeasures have been implemented and evaluated against F&S.
Code has been implemented enabling a fairness-aware scheduler (e.g., VTC-style fair queuing) on top of the vLLM serving backend, penalizing tenants that consume excessive KV/decoding resources.
Code has been implemented enabling a priority queue scheduler that de-prioritizes requests predicted to have long outputs, following the countermeasure described in Section 7.

Code has been implemented that evaluates an adaptive F&S adversary against the fairness/priority schedulers, including a variant that fragments large requests into many short high-priority requests to bypass the priority penalty.

Code has been implemented that measures TTFT/TPOT degradation for legitimate long-context (benign) users under aggressive fairness settings, demonstrating the reported starvation trade-off for benign complex tasks.
Behavioral analysis defense based on per-user output-to-input token ratios (Appendix E.2) has been implemented and evaluated.

Code has been implemented that tracks per-tenant output-to-input token ratios and generation-length statistics over a sliding window and flags tenants whose ratio consistently exceeds a configurable threshold.

Code has been implemented that applies rate-limiting or temporary isolation to flagged tenants and re-evaluates F&S attack effectiveness (TTFT, TPOT, preemption count, cost) under this behavioral defense.
A consolidated countermeasure comparison summarizing the residual effectiveness of F&S against each defense has been produced.

depends_on: Main Attack Effectiveness Results (Table 1 and Fig. 9)
